strengths: The paper addresses a genuine and timely gap: the theoretical understanding of how imperfect verifiers affect test-time scaling. The connection between verifier scaling behavior and the classical ROC curve is elegant and provides a unifying lens.

The theoretical results are clean and well-organized: Proposition 1 links local scaling to the ROC slope, Corollary 1 and Proposition 2 characterize the low- and high-compute regimes via the top-right and bottom-left corners of the ROC curve, and Proposition 3 (de-emergence) formalizes the intuitive claim that small-scale performance cannot predict large-scale performance. Theorem 1 showing convergence of BoN and rejection sampling to the same asymptotic accuracy is a satisfying unifying result.

The BoN analysis (Proposition 4) is nontrivial: expressing BoN accuracy via a generalized AUC-type functional (using Scherlis' interpretation) and showing BoN depends on global ROC properties while rejection sampling depends only on local geometry is an interesting contrast. The monotonicity proof for concave ROC curves (via hinge-function density argument) is technically careful.

The empirical validation is well-matched to the theory: the paper precisely predicts scaling curves from estimated per-question ROC curves and shows good agreement with x-marked predictions and confidence intervals, across multiple generator/verifier pairs (Qwen3, Llama families) on GSM8K. The discrete-score extension (Appendix B) thoughtfully bridges theory and the practice of LLM verifiers with coarse scores.
Writing is generally clear; proofs in the appendix appear correct (e.g., dominated convergence argument in Lemma 5, the density argument in Lemma 4).

Practically relevant takeaways: rejection sampling is more compute-efficient than BoN at fixed accuracy but harder to control/parallelize; verifier quality near the origin (conservative thresholds) governs asymptotic performance; the 'hardness of generation vs verification' remark (Remark 1) is a nice conceptual observation.
weaknesses: Scope of empirical validation is narrow: all experiments are on GSM8K, and the main analysis focuses on only 3 specific test questions (i = 2, 7, 8) chosen because they are hard. Broader benchmark coverage (e.g., MATH, coding with unit tests, other domains) and aggregate (dataset-level) analysis would substantially strengthen the empirical claims.

The analysis is per-instance (fixed query q), while most practical interest in test-time scaling concerns aggregate benchmark accuracy over a distribution of questions. The relationship between the per-question ROC-based theory and dataset-level scaling laws (e.g., heavy-tailed difficulty mixtures as in Schaeffer et al.) is not explored, which limits the applicability of the results to the scaling-law discussions the paper cites.

Only two very simple resampling methods (BoN and threshold-based rejection sampling) are analyzed. More modern or practical schemes (verifier-weighted sampling, process reward models, sequential/multi-round rejection sampling with adaptive thresholds) are not covered, and the paper gives little prescriptive guidance for verifier design or threshold selection beyond the qualitative conclusions.

Some results are relatively close to known observations: the precision-based accuracy of rejection sampling (Eq. 3) is essentially standard (as the authors note via [12]), and the asymptotic convergence of both methods could be seen as anticipated. The novelty rests mainly on the ROC-based characterization and the de-emergence result, which, while neat, is an impossibility statement rather than an actionable tool.

Verifier scores come from LLM-as-judge prompting with very coarse discrete scores (0-10), and per-question ROC curves are estimated from 10k samples with some instances at very low accuracy (e.g., 5.9%, 6.7%), raising concerns about estimation quality of the ROC slope near the origin, which the theory shows is decisive for asymptotic performance. Sensitivity of conclusions to ROC estimation error is not quantified.

The theory assumes conditional independence of samples from the generator and a fixed ground-truth labeling function; real LLM self-consistency and correlated sampling modes (e.g., near-duplicate answers) could deviate from these assumptions, but no experiments probe these robustness issues.

Comparison with concurrent work (Huang et al. [36]) is discussed but the relationship—what their score/reward-distance framework predicts vs. what the ROC framework adds—is only sketched; a direct empirical or formal comparison would sharpen the positioning.

strengths: The paper addresses a genuinely relevant question — how imperfect verifiers affect test-time scaling — and the ROC-curve framing is clean and unifying, connecting BoN and rejection sampling scaling to a classical ML concept.

The core results are internally consistent: the characterization of early scaling by the top-right corner of the ROC curve (Corollary 1), the asymptotic limit by the slope at the origin (Proposition 2, Theorem 1), and the impossibility result (Proposition 3) form a coherent story with a practically meaningful takeaway (small-scale results do not extrapolate).
Proposition 4's integral representation of BoN accuracy and the monotonicity proof via hinge-function approximation (Appendix C.5) are the most technically substantive part of the paper.
The extension of the theory to discrete verifier scores (Appendix B) is a sensible practical patch, and experiments include multiple generator/verifier pairs with confidence intervals.
The paper is well-written and clearly structured, and the theoretical predictions match the empirical curves well in the reported figures.
weaknesses: Limited technical depth: most core results (Equations 2–4, Propositions 1–2, Corollary 1, Corollary 2) follow from elementary Bayes' rule, geometric distributions, and standard calculus (Taylor/L'Hôpital). The genuinely new mathematical content is concentrated in Proposition 4 and its monotonicity proof, making the overall contribution feel thin for a top-tier venue.

The empirical validation is close to circular: the 'predicted' theoretical curves are computed from the per-question ROC curve estimated from the same 10,000 scored samples used to produce the empirical scaling curves. Given the theory is essentially a deterministic function of the empirical ROC, the match is expected rather than a strong independent test of the theory.

Empirical scope is very narrow: only three GSM8K questions (i ∈ {2, 7, 8}), a single domain, and small open-weight models. No evaluation on a second domain (e.g., coding with unit-test verifiers) or on aggregate (benchmark-level) scaling, so the breadth of the claims is not supported.

The compute model assumes constant cost per sample and ignores verifier cost, even though in the experiments the verifier is itself an LLM whose per-call cost is comparable to (or larger than) generation. The claimed compute comparisons between rejection sampling and BoN are therefore not directly meaningful for the practical setting studied.

The analysis assumes access to the Pareto-optimal thresholded classifier h_F at every false-positive rate F; practical threshold selection on estimated scores can deviate from the ROC frontier, and the paper does not discuss robustness to this gap.

Some proof details are loose: the extension of monotonicity (Lemma 6) to non-integer p introduces ad hoc 'fractional' random variables with hand-waved coupling arguments, and the concentration step in the proof of Theorem 1 relies on a t → 0 sandwich that should be stated more carefully.

Positioning against closely related work could be sharper: the connection to precision-recall tradeoffs and partial AUC is acknowledged, but the delta relative to Huang et al. [36] and Song et al. [12] is mainly a reframing via ROC geometry rather than a fundamentally new analysis.

No mention of code or artifact release, and the discrete-score smoothing (Definition 2) injects randomness into the score; the claim that this 'does not meaningfully affect' BoN performance deserves quantification rather than assertion.

The 'de-emergence' impossibility result (Proposition 3), while conceptually appealing, is a fairly direct consequence of the freedom to choose the ROC curve near the origin, and its practical implications for real verifier selection are not explored.

strengths: Addresses a timely and under-theorized question: how verifier imperfection affects test-time scaling, connecting it to the classical ROC curve framework in a clean and conceptually satisfying way.

The theoretical results are elegant and substantive: Proposition 1 shows the local slope of the ROC curve governs the accuracy-compute derivative for rejection sampling; Propositions 2 and Theorem 1 show that the large-compute limit of BOTH rejection sampling and BoN is determined solely by the ROC slope at the origin; Proposition 3 formalizes the impossibility of extrapolating large-scale performance from small-scale results ('de-emergence').

The proofs (Appendix C) are careful and self-contained, including a non-trivial monotonicity argument for BoN (Lemma 2 via hinge-function density/duality arguments) and a rigorous dominated-convergence treatment for Theorem 1.

The theory is predictive, not just descriptive: the closed-form predictions (Equations 2-5) are validated quantitatively against empirical curves with 95% CIs across multiple generator/verifier pairs (Qwen3, Llama families) on GSM8K.

Practical implications are clearly articulated: (i) rejection sampling is more compute-efficient than BoN at low compute, (ii) early scaling does not predict asymptotic scaling, and (iii) both methods share the same accuracy ceiling set by T'(0).
The relaxation of the continuous-score assumption (Appendix B, matching sklearn's ROC convention) shows attention to the gap between theory and practice.
weaknesses: The empirical validation is quite narrow: experiments are restricted to GSM8K and, in the main text, essentially to a handful of hand-selected test questions (i in {2,7,8}) chosen specifically to exhibit interesting behavior. Broader coverage (aggregated per-question results, other domains like coding where verifiers are widely used) would substantially strengthen the claims.

The analysis is per-instance: accuracy and ROC curves are defined conditional on a single fixed query q, while aggregate benchmark scaling (the practically relevant regime) requires additional assumptions about the distribution over instance difficulties (cf. Schaeffer et al.). The paper does not address how the per-instance theory aggregates.

Compute is modeled only as the number of samples drawn; verifier compute is treated as free and identical across methods, and samples are assumed i.i.d. with constant per-sample cost. In practice, BoN and rejection sampling have very different verification costs, which weakens the practical force of the compute comparisons.

Some theoretical assumptions are strong: concavity/differentiability of the ROC curve and Assumption 1 (density of scores). While Appendix B handles discrete scores, the empirical verifiers produce only ~11 discrete score values, and the paper relies on the smoothed-score workaround rather than directly analyzing the discrete setting.

Related work on BoN theory (e.g., Huang et al. [36]) is discussed but the paper does not provide a crisp formal comparison delineating what is new relative to that concurrent work beyond the binary-reward/ROC framing.
No discussion of code/artifact release, which limits reproducibility of the experimental portion.
The impossibility result (Proposition 3), while neat, is arguably intuitive; its practical significance for LLM scaling decisions could be better motivated with a concrete use case.

strengths: Clear and useful theoretical contribution: the paper gives an exact characterization of instance-level test-time scaling for both Rejection Sampling (RS) and Best-of-N (BoN) in terms of the verifier's ROC curve, including elegant results linking low- and high-compute scaling to the local geometry of the ROC curve (Propositions 1-2, Theorem 1).

The impossibility results (Propositions 3 and 7) formalizing that high-compute performance cannot be extrapolated from low-compute observations are novel, practically relevant, and well-motivated by the empirical findings in Figure 1.
The connection between RS and KL-regularized RL (Proposition 4) is a nice bonus result that ties the analysis to recent post-training practice and gives the high-compute limit broader significance.

The BoN analysis is technically non-trivial: the integral formula via a Scherlis-style generalization of AUC (Proposition 5), the layer-cake / Beta-distribution reformulation (Proposition 8, Theorem 2), and the convex-combination-of-hinges characterization in the appendix show genuine mathematical depth.

Empirical validation is appropriate: per-instance predictions match theory closely across multiple generator/verifier combinations, aggregate results on full GSM8K/MATH500 confirm the qualitative takeaways (RS outperforms BoN at fixed compute; convergence at high compute; non-extrapolability), and the appendix handles the practically important case of discrete verifier scores.

Good positioning relative to prior work (Song et al. for RS under ROC, Huang et al. bounds via MSE, Brown et al./Schaeffer et al. for pass@N), clearly articulating what is new: ground-truth accuracy under imperfect verifiers, BoN characterization, and impossibility results.
weaknesses: Limited novelty in parts: the characterization of RS accuracy via precision at a threshold and the ROC framing is closely related to Song et al. [15], which the authors acknowledge; the genuinely new material is concentrated in the BoN analysis and the impossibility results, so the overall delta over [15] may be seen as incremental by some reviewers.

The theory assumes a fixed query with a fixed binary correctness label, so results are per-instance; the extension to aggregate accuracy over datasets is only empirical, and the paper itself concedes that distributional assumptions could change the conclusions. Reasoning-model verifiers and continuous rewards (e.g., partial credit) are out of scope.

The empirical evaluation, while consistent with the theory, is somewhat limited: per-instance validation covers a small, selectively chosen set of GSM8K questions (selected as the first incorrectly answered ones), verifier scores are elicited via a single prompting scheme (0-10 scale, averaged over 5 samples), and no cost accounting beyond sample counts (e.g., verification tokens vs. generation tokens) is provided, which matters for the RS vs. BoN compute comparison since verification calls are made repeatedly in RS.

The impossibility results, while correct, are in a sense expected (worst-case extrapolation from a finite prefix of a curve is impossible without regularity assumptions), so their practical impact depends on the reader's priors; the paper could do more to quantify how misleading extrapolation is on realistic ROC curves rather than via worst-case constructions.

Practical applicability of RS's compute advantage is somewhat undercut by known practical disadvantages (sequential sampling, indirect budget control) which are mentioned only in passing; a head-to-head wall-clock or FLOP-based comparison would strengthen the claim that RS is preferable in practice.

Writing is generally clear but notation-heavy (T, F, C, A, bars and tildes); several propositions could be stated more accessibly, and some proofs in the appendix are lengthy relative to the insight they deliver.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant and timely question — how verifier imperfection governs test-time scaling — and connects it cleanly to the classical ROC framework.

The theoretical development is coherent and largely self-contained: accuracy/compute of RS is characterized locally (Prop 1, Eq. 7), the high-compute limit is tied to the ROC slope at the origin (Prop 2, Thm 1), and an integral representation of BoN accuracy via the ROC curve is derived (Prop 5, Thm 2).
The impossibility results (Props 3 and 7), showing that high-compute performance cannot be extrapolated from low-compute observations, are a useful cautionary message for practitioners.

Empirical validation is reasonably careful: per-instance predictions are verified on multiple generator/verifier pairs (Qwen3, Llama) and aggregate trends are confirmed on GSM8K and MATH500, with prediction errors reported and CIs given.
The treatment of discrete verifier scores (Appendix E) and the connection to KL-regularized RL (Prop 4) add practical and conceptual completeness.
weaknesses: Limited novelty relative to prior work: the core observation that RS accuracy equals the precision of the thresholded verifier, and its ROC-based characterization, is already in Song et al. [15], as the authors acknowledge. The genuinely new material (BoN integral formula, RS-vs-BoN dominance, non-extrapolability) is incremental and, in places, follows from relatively standard arguments (e.g., Prop 4 is a direct consequence of the known optimal KL-regularized RL solution).

The non-extrapolability results (Props 3, 7) are construction-based impossibility statements of a fairly expected type: without assumptions on the ROC curve near the origin, of course small-scale behavior cannot determine the limit. The practical takeaway (don't extrapolate scaling curves) will not surprise most readers.

Several key results require concavity of the ROC curve (Props 6, 8, 9), but real verifier ROC curves are shown to be non-concave in the experiments (e.g., Llama-3.2-3B in Fig. 4); the paper only informally argues the conclusions still hold empirically, leaving a gap between theory and practice.

The theory is strictly per-instance (fixed query, binary ground truth), so its applicability to aggregate accuracy — the quantity practitioners actually care about — is only conjectured and tested empirically; no aggregate theory is provided.

The empirical scope is narrow: two math benchmarks, small open-weight models, simple threshold/argmax resampling, and a fixed prompt-based 0-10 scoring verifier. No experiments with reward-model verifiers, process verifiers, or reasoning-style test-time scaling, limiting external validity of the 'verifier imperfection' claims.

Predicting per-instance performance requires estimating the full ROC curve from 1000 labeled samples per query, which is a strong requirement; the practical value of the 'prediction' framework when ground-truth labels are unavailable (the motivating regime) is not demonstrated.

The RS compute cap (25 samples) in the aggregate experiments truncates the high-compute regime precisely where the paper's main theoretical distinctions (Prop 2, Thm 1) manifest, weakening the empirical support for the high-compute claims at the dataset level.

strengths: The paper provides a clean and complete theoretical characterization of verifier-based test-time scaling: both Rejection Sampling (RS) and Best-of-N (BoN) accuracy are shown to be fully determined by the generator accuracy and the verifier's ROC curve (Propositions 1 and 5), connecting scaling behavior to local (top-right / bottom-left corner) and global ROC geometry.

The negative/impossibility results are valuable and practically relevant: Propositions 3 and 7 formally show that high-compute performance cannot be extrapolated from small-scale observations, a caution directly relevant to practitioners who fit scaling curves.

The comparison between methods is well executed: Proposition 6 proves RS outperforms BoN at fixed compute under concave ROC assumptions, Theorem 1 shows both converge to the same limit, and the large-N limit formula (T'(0)π / (T'(0)π + 1−π)) is simple and interpretable.
The connection to KL-regularized RL (Proposition 4), showing the optimal RL policy converges to the RS distribution as β→0, gives the BoN/RS analysis broader relevance to reasoning-model training.

The empirical validation is convincing for what it sets out to do: measured ROC curves from real LLM verifiers (Qwen3, Llama) accurately predict per-instance RS and BoN accuracy across GSM8K and MATH500, and aggregate experiments confirm the theoretical trends. Appendices include detailed proofs, a notation table, discrete-score extensions, and prompts, supporting reproducibility.
The writing is clear, the setup is well-motivated, and the limitations and non-concave-ROC caveats are handled honestly (including the extension in Appendix E).
weaknesses: Novelty is incremental on the RS side: the authors themselves note that Song et al. [15] already characterized RS compute-scaling via the ROC curve and observed the precision-of-accepted-samples interpretation. The core RS results (Equations 4-7, Propositions 1-2) largely formalize and extend that prior work; the genuinely new material is the BoN characterization, the impossibility results, and Proposition 6.

The theory is per-instance (fixed query), while practical relevance concerns aggregate performance; the aggregate experiments (Figure 5) require practical workarounds (capping RS at 25 samples, null outputs on rejection) that mean the theory is only partially validated in the aggregate setting, and the concavity assumption is empirically violated in places.

Compute is measured purely as number of samples/generations, ignoring verifier cost (which differs across methods and verifiers) and treating verification as free; this limits the strength of the RS-dominates-BoN conclusion for real deployments.

Experimental scope is narrow: only two math benchmarks (GSM8K, MATH500), binary ground-truth labels, verifier scores obtained via a single prompted 0-10 scale, and no safety/coding or open-ended domains where verifier imperfection is arguably most consequential.

The high-compute-limit analysis (Theorem 1) relies on a deterministic-surrogate argument plus concentration, and its assumptions (continuous differentiability of the ROC near 0, absolutely continuous scores) require nontrivial machinery (Appendix E smoothing) to apply to the discrete LLM scores actually used in experiments, so the theory-practice bridge is somewhat engineered.

While the predictions fit well on showcased questions, the aggregate accuracy differences between RS and BoN in Figure 5 are small and within confidence intervals in parts of the MATH500 plot, so the practical significance of the fixed-compute advantage is not fully established.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated research question: the paper addresses a genuine gap — the theoretical understanding of how verifier imperfection affects test-time scaling of resampling methods (RS and BoN), which has mostly been studied under the perfect-verifier assumption.

The central technical contribution is clean and elegant: instance-level accuracy of both BoN and RS is fully characterized by the generator's initial accuracy π and the verifier's ROC curve (Propositions 1 and 5). The integral representation of BoN accuracy over the ROC curve (Proposition 5) is a nice result that recovers the known pass@N formula as a special case.

The results are well-structured around practically meaningful takeaways: (i) RS outperforms BoN at fixed compute for concave ROC curves (Proposition 6), (ii) both methods converge to the same limit determined by T'(0) (Proposition 2, Theorem 1), and (iii) a formal impossibility result showing high-compute performance cannot be predicted from low-compute observations (Propositions 3 and 7). These negative results have real practical value for practitioners who extrapolate scaling trends.

The connection to KL-regularized RL (Proposition 4), showing that the optimal RL policy converges to RS as regularization vanishes, extends the relevance of the theory beyond pure resampling to reasoning-style methods.

Experiments are carefully designed to directly validate the theory: per-instance predictions from estimated ROC curves match empirical RS/BoN accuracy closely (Figures 1, 4, E.2-E.6), and aggregate results on GSM8K/MATH500 (plus GPQA and HumanEval+ in the appendix) confirm the qualitative takeaways. Capped Rejection Sampling is a simple, practically useful methodological contribution that emerges from the analysis.

Proofs are complete and largely self-contained (Appendix D), with appropriate mathematical rigor (dominated convergence, layer-cake representations, careful treatment of score ties via randomization).

The paper is clearly written, with good figures that illustrate the theory (e.g., Figure 3 showing how the top-right vs. bottom-left corners of the ROC curve govern different compute regimes), and honest discussion of limitations in the Discussion section.
weaknesses: Some results are relatively unsurprising or incremental when viewed carefully: RS accuracy is simply the precision of the threshold classifier (acknowledged as observed by Song et al. [15]), and the BoN integral representation builds on known connections between AUROC and ranking metrics (Scherlis [39]). The main novelty lies in packaging and consequences (scaling limits, impossibility of extrapolation) rather than fundamentally new mathematical machinery.

The theory assumes a fixed query with i.i.d. samples and a fixed binary ground-truth labeling, which is a strong simplification: real verifiers are stochastic, correlated across samples, and many verification settings (e.g., process rewards, reasoning methods with variable-length responses) fall outside the model. The extension of the main conclusions to RL is only heuristic (via Proposition 4 plus a citation to Xiong et al.).

The equivalence result assumes access to the exact per-query ROC curve; in practice this must be estimated from finite samples, especially in the bottom-left corner (F ≈ 0) that governs the high-compute limit — precisely where empirical estimation is hardest. The paper does not analyze how estimation error in the ROC curve near the origin propagates to prediction error in the high-compute limit.

Experimental scope is somewhat limited: only Qwen3 and Llama model families, and mostly math benchmarks, with the strongest quantitative per-instance validation on a small hand-picked set of GSM8K questions. The aggregate experiments require heuristics (difficulty-based thresholds, capped RS) that are somewhat ad hoc and not covered by the theory.

There is a disclosed methodological inconsistency (Appendix E: random-seed issue causing few-shot prompts to be resampled per generation in the individual-question experiments but per question in aggregate experiments), which weakens strict comparability across the two experimental setups.

The practical actionability of the impossibility results is limited: while the paper convincingly shows that extrapolation fails in the worst case, it does not provide guidance on what auxiliary assumptions or measurements would make extrapolation possible — a natural next step that is deferred to future work.

Compute accounting compares methods primarily by expected number of samples/generations; while the Wald's-identity argument in C.1 extends this to expected tokens, verifier and generator costs differ substantially in practice (a 32B verifier is much more expensive per call than a 1.7B generator), and the paper's compute metric does not reflect this asymmetry, which could affect the RS-vs-BoN comparison quantitatively.

strengths: The core idea is elegant: connecting per-instance test-time scaling of rejection sampling (RS) and Best-of-N (BoN) to the geometry of the verifier's ROC curve is a clean, unifying framing that yields exact, checkable predictions.

The theory is complete and largely self-contained: the derivation of compute cost (Eq. 4), accuracy (Eq. 5-6), the integral representation of BoN accuracy (Proposition 5), and the high-compute limits (Proposition 2, Theorem 1) are all proven in detail, with care taken over ties, distributional transforms, and measure-theoretic details.

The impossibility results (Propositions 3 and 7) are a genuinely useful and non-obvious takeaway: they formally justify the common practical intuition that low-compute scaling trends cannot be extrapolated to high compute, which has direct relevance for how practitioners report and interpret scaling curves.
The connection between RS and KL-regularized RL (Proposition 4) is a nice touch that broadens the potential applicability of the theoretical limits beyond pure resampling.

The experiments are well designed to validate the theory: per-query predictions from estimated ROC curves match empirical RS/BoN accuracies closely, and the aggregate results on GSM8K, MATH500 (plus GPQA and HumanEval+ in the appendix) qualitatively confirm the main takeaways, including the practical 'Capped RS' hybrid.
weaknesses: Practical significance is limited: RS is rarely the method of choice in practice because its compute cannot be controlled directly and parallelization is hard, and the paper itself acknowledges this. The RS-beats-BoN result, while clean, may have modest impact on how frontier systems actually allocate test-time compute.

The analysis is confined to binary ground-truth rewards and a fixed query, so all statements are per-instance; the aggregate behavior is only validated heuristically, and the paper's own heuristics (difficulty-based thresholds, capped RS) are ad hoc and not covered by the theory.

Several results feel close to expected: that RS dominates BoN at fixed compute for concave ROCs and that both converge to the same limit are plausible a priori, and the value of the paper rests heavily on the impossibility/extrapolation results being novel relative to prior work (e.g., Stroebl et al., Huang et al., Song et al.), where the added precision over existing bounds needs to be weighed carefully.

Empirical validation is narrow in places: the headline per-query predictions rely on ROC curves estimated from ~1000 samples on a small hand-selected set of GSM8K questions, and some results (e.g., Figure 4, Figure E.6) use low-accuracy generators where the regime is somewhat degenerate; the significance of specific test questions is not systematically justified.

The concavity assumption does substantial work in the theory, yet real LLM verifiers exhibit non-concave ROCs (acknowledged for Llama-3.2-3B), and the gap between idealized assumptions and observed curves is not deeply analyzed.
Scope of models and benchmarks is modest (small open-weight generators, Qwen3/Llama verifiers), so claims about generality to modern reasoning-model pipelines remain extrapolative.

strengths: The paper fills a genuine gap: prior theoretical work on test-time scaling largely assumed oracle verifiers (pass@N analysis) or gave only bounds (e.g., Huang et al. via MSE), whereas this work provides an exact characterization of BoN and RS accuracy via the verifier's ROC curve, which is an elegant and natural object for this problem.

The main takeaways are crisp and actionable: (i) for concave ROC curves RS dominates BoN at fixed compute while both converge to the same accuracy limit determined by the ROC slope at the origin (Propositions 2, 6, Theorem 1); (ii) low-compute performance cannot be extrapolated to high-compute regimes (Propositions 3 and 7). The impossibility results are rigorously formalized rather than just asserted.

The connection between KL-regularized RL and rejection sampling (Proposition 4) is a nice bonus that suggests the high-compute limit may also bound RL-based reasoning, connecting the resampling analysis to a much broader class of methods.

The theoretical predictions are quantitatively validated per-instance: estimated ROC curves from 1000 samples predict RS/BoN accuracy with absolute errors below one percentage point in the shown cases, and aggregate experiments on GSM8K, MATH500, GPQA, and HumanEval+ confirm the qualitative claims across multiple generator/verifier pairs.

The paper is well written and well organized; proofs (in the appendix) appear careful, including non-trivial technical work such as the distributional-transform argument for the BoN integral (Lemma 2), the dominated-convergence analysis for Theorem 1, and the constructive extrapolation results. Practical side contributions like 'Capped Rejection Sampling' add value.
Related work is comprehensive and positioning relative to Stroebl et al., Song et al., Chen et al., and Huang et al. is clearly articulated.
weaknesses: The scope is limited to per-instance, binary-correctness settings with iid sampling; many practical test-time setups (aggregated metrics, non-binary rewards, dependent samples, sequential/adaptive resampling) fall outside the theory, and the aggregate experiments require heuristic thresholding whose justification is empirical rather than theoretical.

The key dominance result (Proposition 6) requires concave ROC curves, but the paper's own experiments exhibit non-concave verifier ROCs (e.g., Llama-3.2-3B in Figure 4); the theory therefore does not cover some of the very cases it demonstrates, and behavior under general non-concave ROCs is not characterized.

Compute accounting assumes each verification costs like one sample (with a Wald's-equation remark); in practice verifier cost can differ substantially from generator cost (e.g., long chain-of-thought verifiers), and the paper does not explore sensitivity of the RS-vs-BoN conclusions to this modeling choice.

Empirical validation is mostly on small-to-mid-size open models (Qwen3-1.7B/4B generators, GSM8K/MATH500), and per-instance validation covers only a handful of hand-picked questions (the first incorrect GSM8K questions for the generator); this raises some concern about selection and generalization of the per-instance fit claims.

Several results (e.g., Propositions 3 and 7, the negative extrapolation results) formalize intuitions that many readers may find unsurprising; the incremental conceptual novelty over Stroebl et al.'s empirical observations is the rigor and exactness, which some reviewers may view as modest.
No explicit statement about code or artifact release is given, which limits reproducibility of the experimental pipeline (few-shot prompting, 5x score averaging, difficulty heuristics).

Minor presentation issues: Figure 3 is synthetic-only; some experimental details (random-seed issue affecting few-shot resampling) are relegated to the appendix and could confound comparisons between per-instance and aggregate settings.
